passage:
Monday. Seema stepped off the night bus in Chennai with her bag held in front of her. She asked the auto driver where the guesthouse lane was, then the flower seller, then the man at the tea stall. Two pointed left, one right. She followed the two, and checked once more at the corner shop.
Wednesday. A stranger said, "Come, I'll show you a shortcut." She thanked him, said she would ask at the shop, and did.
Friday. Her colleague Jahnavi laughed at her list of directions. "Three people? Two of them would have done." But the route was correct every time.

qa.a: Seema asked the auto driver, the flower seller and the man at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Seema probably feeling when the stranger offered a shortcut on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably cautious and a little uneasy, since she thanked him and chose to check at the shop instead.

qa.q: What did Seema do to reduce the risk of a wrong turn?
qa.a: She asked several people, compared their answers and checked again at the corner shop, keeping her bag in front.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Seema's habit of asking three people?
qa.a: Jahnavi finds it funny and says two would do, but sees that Seema's routes were correct each time.

passage: Beta, I am Mehak, and at twenty-four I travelled to Varanasi with a fellow traveller, Dhruv, who said, "Ask one person, everyone is friendly." Many are, but I asked three people for the way to the ghat: a chaiwala, a shop owner and a woman selling flowers. Two answers matched, and one man who had joined us said he would take us by a different lane. It was longer, and crowded. My bag was zipped and in front of me. At the end of the lane, Dhruv put his hand to his back pocket and found it empty. I checked answers against each other after that, and Dhruv never again trusted a single voice.

qa.q: How many people did Mehak ask for the way to the ghat?
qa.a: Mehak asked three people for the way to the ghat, a chaiwala, a shop owner and a woman selling flowers.

qa.q: What was Mehak probably feeling when a man joined them and offered a different lane?
qa.a: Mehak was probably cautious and alert, since the bag was zipped and held in front and the answers had been checked against each other.

qa.q: What choice by Mehak made the journey safer?
qa.a: Mehak asked several people, checked their answers against each other and kept the bag zipped and in front.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's view of asking for directions have changed after the pocket?
qa.a: Dhruv learned that friendly help is common but one voice may not be enough, and he stopped trusting a single answer.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a traveller who asked several people, compared answers and kept valuables close, against a companion who trusted one voice.

passage: Saturday. Found Papa's old torch in the drawer that doesn't work. I asked Keerthana didi if I could open it. She said yes, but first took the battery out and gave me the small screwdriver from her box. Inside there was a spring, a tiny round bulb and a metal strip! I pressed the strip and the spring pushed back. My heart went boom. I took out everything and put it on the table in a line. Then I could not put it back. The spring jumped away twice. Keerthana didi found it under the cupboard. We put it together, and on the third try the light came on. I clapped. Arohi

passage: The alarm clock in Binita's house in the village had stopped years ago and lay on the shelf like a dead beetle. On Sunday, her older brother Eshaan gave her a small screwdriver and a plate. "Unscrew only the back, and put every screw on the plate." Binita worked slowly. Inside were wheels with tiny teeth and a coiled spring. She turned one wheel with her finger, and another wheel moved. "They're holding hands!" she whispered. When she tried to close it again, the wheels would not line up. Dada came and showed her where the small wheel fitted. The clock ticked for a minute. Binita listened with her head on her arm.

First he switched off the fan and the main switch and stuck tape over it with a note. Preeti asked why he loosened the blades one by one. "So they balance," he said, and showed her the small gap on one. She watched his hands more than his face. When the fan ran quietly, she said, "I could do that." He smiled and said, "Next time, you can hold the screwdriver." I have never seen her stand so straight. Noor

He told me to rough up the rubber, and why the glue needs to dry a little before the patch. I did the patch with my own hands. It looked ugly but held air. I rode round the lane three times. Nobody had to tell me I was proud. Afreen

passage: The tap in our kitchen dripped all night, and I decided to fix it with a video. First I turned off the water at the small valve, opened the tap to empty it, and laid a cloth over the drain. I unscrewed the cap, swapped the old rubber washer for a new one, and turned the water back on. No drip! I was so proud I made tea for my flatmate Varun and showed him. Then, feeling brave, I tried the leaking joint of the pipe under the sink. The leak got worse. I turned off the valve, put a bucket under it and called a plumber. I had learned which jobs are mine. Asif

passage: Repair shop note. Sarita came in on Saturday with a phone in two pieces. She had watched a video and tried to replace the cracked screen herself. She had pried the glass up with a kitchen knife, and it had cracked further; the thin cable was torn. She stood there red-eyed, quiet, half proud of having tried. I told her plainly that the screen swap is a job for a shop because the battery sits right under it and can be damaged. I asked her to bring a broken old phone next time to practise on. She nodded and asked if she could watch me. I said yes. Sharmila, shop owner

passage: Kamal had rewired a socket once, badly but successfully, and since then he believed he knew electricity. When the bulb holder in the verandah began to spark, he climbed on a stool with a screwdriver and did not bother to go to the switchboard. "It's only a holder," he told his mother. The tingle that ran up his arm made him drop the screwdriver, and his heart hammered. He came down, furious with himself. Kishore, the licensed electrician from the next village, came that evening, switched off the main first, checked it with a tester, and replaced the holder. "Some jobs are not for guessing," he said quietly. Kamal did not argue.

qa.q: What did Kamal say about the bulb holder?
qa.a: Kamal said, "It's only a holder."

qa.a: Kishore, the licensed electrician, switched off the main, checked with a tester and replaced the holder, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Kamal's mother have felt when she heard him say it was only a holder?
qa.a: Kamal's mother was probably worried and alarmed, and perhaps relieved when Kishore arrived to do the job safely.

grounding: Shows an adult with a little experience fixing wiring without switching off first, a warning tingle, and a licensed person as the wise choice.

passage: Jana had fixed a dripping tap and a rattling shelf, so a faint gas smell behind the cooker seemed like the next small job. In her flat in Vienna she pulled the cooker forward, gripped the rubber hose and started to twist the clamp. "How hard can it be?" The smell grew stronger. Selin, her neighbour, knocked to borrow sugar and stopped. "That's gas. Stop. Don't touch any switch." Jana's hands were shaking. They opened the windows, turned off the gas at the wall valve, and left the flat. Selin phoned the gas company from the stairwell. The technician who came said the clamp had been loosened.

qa.q: What did Selin come to borrow?
qa.a: Selin came to borrow sugar.

qa.q: What was Jana feeling after she heard Selin say "That's gas"?
qa.a: Jana was frightened and shaken, and her overconfidence changed to alarm as her hands shook.

qa.q: What safe steps did Jana and Selin take?
qa.a: They opened the windows, turned off the gas at the wall valve, left the flat, avoided switches and phoned the gas company from the stairwell.

qa.q: Why might Selin have said "Stop" so firmly?
qa.a: Selin smelled gas and knew that a spark or another wrong move could be dangerous, so the firm tone came from concern for both of them.

grounding: Shows an adult with a little success fixing a gas problem overconfidently, and a licensed person as the wise choice.

passage:
Dear Sachin,
The washing machine stopped last week, and the technician who came said the main board had burnt out. He quoted a big price and said it was urgent. I felt helpless because I could not check. But I remembered what you said, so I asked him to show me the fault. He pointed at the board and said, "See?" I saw only a green plate. I said I would think about it, and asked for the quote in writing. Then I called another repairer, who found a loose belt and fixed it in half an hour for a tiny fraction of the price. I felt relieved and a bit foolish. Thank you for the tip. Bhupen

qa.a: The first technician said the main board had burnt out.

qa.q: What steps protected Bhupen from needless work or overcharging?

grounding: Shows a householder feeling helpless when a technician names a problem and price they cannot verify, then asking for the fault to be shown and a second opinion.

passage: The geyser stopped one Monday and a man came from the shop. He said the element had failed and quoted a price. I stood there in the bathroom doorway feeling small, because I do not know what an element is. Vijay, you asked what I do in these moments. I say, Could you show me? He held up a blackened rod and said, See, it's burnt. Fine. But I asked to keep the old one when it was replaced, and I asked a neighbour, whose husband does repairs, what a fair price is. It was close. I paid, and the geyser worked. Not knowing is normal; asking to be shown is my small armour. Urmila

passage: It was ten at night, the shops were shut, and tomorrow the family was coming for lunch. The kitchen cabinet door hung by one screw. He tightened the loose hinge screw, then wiped a drop of oil on the hinge so it would not squeak. His neighbour Jaya, who had come to borrow the drill, watched. "You always have everything." "I put it back after every job," he said. She left with the drill, and he wrote it in the book by the toolbox.

passage: On Sunday mornings, Chetan gave his flat fifteen minutes. He took the toolbox from its shelf, where the labelled trays held screws by size, and tightened the wobbly chair leg with the right screwdriver. He cleaned the water filter, put a drop of oil on the door hinge and pumped up the tyre of his scooter. His sister Preeti, sitting with her tea, said, "You do this every week? For what?" "So it doesn't cost me more later," Chetan said. Three weeks later Preeti's landlord asked for a big bill for her cracked filter. Chetan's was still fine. She did not tease him again, and borrowed the screwdriver instead.

Monday. Madhuri got her first payment app and paid for the samosa, the bus pass top-up and a game skin without a thought. Tapping felt like nothing.
Wednesday of the next week. At the canteen the app said there was no balance. Madhuri counted the payments, one by one, in a corner, cheeks hot. "It didn't feel like spending."

passage:
"Look, I won a prize," said Keerthana, holding up her phone. "Some desk says approve this and get five thousand."
"Let me see." Tenzin frowned at the screen. "That's a request to take money out of you. See the word collect?"
"But it says urgent, expires in two minutes!"
"That's the trick, they make you rush."
"So I just tap approve?"
"No. You don't know them. You don't approve what you didn't expect."
Keerthana let out a shaky breath. "I'll show Papa."
"Good. And never say your PIN or OTP to anyone."
She closed the message and went to find Papa.

passage: The phone rang at dinner time. A man said he was from my bank and that my account would be blocked in ten minutes unless I gave him the code that had just arrived by message. I put the phone down and told Mummy. She checked with the bank's own number on the card, and there was no problem at all. I still think about how urgent he sounded. Pausing was the whole trick. Chetan
